steps.body: Real floor plans are not single rectangles. The move that handles all of them is the same: break the figure into pieces you already know, find each area, then ADD the pieces that are there and SUBTRACT the ones cut away. A ledger, kept honestly, beats any formula.
Keep the ledger for an L-shaped room.

widget.prompt: A 10 by 8 room has a 3 by 4 alcove cut out of one corner. What floor area remains?

choices.feedback: Correct: 80 square units of room, less the 12 taken by the alcove.
The alcove was ADDED. It is cut away, so its area comes off the total.
That is the room before the alcove was removed — the subtraction has not happened yet.
That is the alcove alone, not the floor that remains.

widget.successFeedback: 68 square units. Subtracting a known piece is often far quicker than slicing the leftover into strips.

predict.prompt: An alcove is cut out of a rectangular room. To find the remaining floor, the alcove's area is…

options.label: Ignored — it does not change the floor

predict.reveal: The ledger's signs are the whole method: pieces present count positive, pieces removed count negative. Getting a sign wrong is the most common composite-area error, and it is visible immediately — the answer comes out larger than the whole rectangle it started from.

explanationVariants: Two rectangles side by side simply add.

widget.prompt: An L-shape splits into a 6 by 4 rectangle and a 5 by 2 rectangle. What is its total area?

commonErrors.feedback: That is the larger piece alone — the 5 by 2 rectangle is still to be added.
That adds the dimensions rather than the areas. Compute each rectangle first.

widget.successFeedback: 34 — cut into knowable pieces, add the ledger.

steps.body: There is usually more than one correct cut. The same L-shape can be sliced vertically or horizontally, or read as a big rectangle with a bite taken out. Every honest route gives the same total — which makes a second method the fastest way to check the first.

explanationVariants: A 9 by 6 rectangle is 54; removing a 2 by 3 corner of 6 leaves 48.

widget.prompt: A 9 by 6 rectangle has a 2 by 3 corner removed. What area remains?

commonErrors.feedback: The corner was added instead of removed — the answer cannot exceed the original 54.
That is the full rectangle; the corner has not been taken off yet.

widget.successFeedback: 48 — and slicing the L into two rectangles would give 48 as well, which is exactly the check worth doing.

explanationVariants: The rectangle is 8×5 = 40 and the triangle (8×3)/2 = 12, totalling 52.
A house shape is a rectangle plus a triangular roof.

widget.prompt: A house outline is an 8 by 5 rectangle topped by a triangle with base 8 and height 3. What is its area?

commonErrors.feedback: The roof was counted as a full rectangle. A triangle is half of base times height: 12, not 24.
That is the walls alone — the roof has not been added.

widget.successFeedback: 52 — pieces of different shapes cause no trouble as long as each is computed with its own rule.

explanationVariants: 12×10 = 120, minus two 3×3 squares of 9 each, leaves 102.
Subtract both cut-outs, not just one.
hints: Start with the whole rectangle before removing anything.
Each cut-out square has area 3×3 = 9, and there are two of them.

widget.prompt: A 12 by 10 panel has TWO 3 by 3 squares cut out. What area remains?

commonErrors.feedback: Only one square was removed. Both cut-outs come off the total.
Neither cut-out has been subtracted yet.

widget.successFeedback: 102 — the ledger scales to any number of pieces, in either direction.

takeaways: Break a composite figure into shapes whose areas you already know.
Pieces present are added; pieces removed are subtracted.
Different valid cuts give the same total, which makes a second method a free check.
